_link.title: I can define tonicity, hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic

options.text: How extracellular solute concentration affects cell volume via osmosis
options.explanation: Tonicity refers to how the solute concentration of a solution relative to a cell determines the direction of osmosis and thus cell volume.

options.text: The speed at which molecules diffuse through a solid membrane wall
options.explanation: Tonicity relates to solute concentration differences, not to the speed of diffusion through solids.

options.text: The total number of organelles found inside a particular living cell
options.explanation: Organelle count is unrelated to tonicity, which concerns solute concentration and osmosis.

options.text: The strength of chemical bonds holding the plasma membrane together
options.explanation: Tonicity is about relative solute concentration, not membrane bond strength.

toLevel2.stem: A hypotonic solution has what characteristic compared to the inside of the cell?

options.text: A lower solute concentration
options.explanation: Hypotonic means the solution outside the cell has a lower solute concentration than the cell's interior.

options.text: A higher solute concentration
options.explanation: A higher solute concentration describes a hypertonic solution, not a hypotonic one.

options.text: An equal solute concentration
options.explanation: Equal solute concentration describes an isotonic solution.

options.text: No solute or water molecules
options.explanation: A hypotonic solution still contains water and may contain some solutes, just fewer than inside the cell.

options.text: The solution has the same solute concentration as inside the cell
options.explanation: Isotonic means equal solute concentration on both sides of the membrane.

options.text: The solution has more solute than is found inside the cell itself
options.explanation: More solute outside describes a hypertonic solution.

options.text: The solution has less solute than is found inside the cell itself
options.explanation: Less solute outside describes a hypotonic solution.

options.text: The solution has been heated to match the cell temperature exactly
options.explanation: Isotonic refers to solute concentration, not temperature.

toLevel2.stem: A hypertonic solution has what characteristic compared to the inside of the cell?

options.text: A higher solute concentration
options.explanation: Hypertonic means the external solution has a higher solute concentration than the cell's interior.

options.text: A lower solute concentration
options.explanation: A lower solute concentration describes a hypotonic solution.

options.text: An equal solute concentration
options.explanation: Equal concentration describes an isotonic solution.

options.text: No water molecules present
options.explanation: A hypertonic solution contains water; it simply has more dissolved solute than the cell.

toLevel2.stem: Tonicity is always described relative to which reference point?

options.text: The cell's internal environment
options.explanation: Tonicity compares the solute concentration of the external solution to the concentration inside the cell.

options.text: Pure distilled water at room temperature
options.explanation: Tonicity is defined relative to the cell's internal solute concentration, not pure water.

options.text: The temperature of the surrounding fluid
options.explanation: Temperature is not the reference for tonicity; it relates to solute concentration.

options.text: The size of the cell membrane pores
options.explanation: Membrane pore size is unrelated to the definition of tonicity.

toLevel2.stem: A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration than the inside of the cell.

options.text: True
options.explanation: By definition, hypertonic means the external solution has more solute than the cell interior.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement correctly defines a hypertonic solution.

toLevel2.stem: An isotonic solution causes a large net movement of water into the cell.

options.text: True
options.explanation: An isotonic solution has equal concentration on both sides, so there is no net movement of water.

options.text: False
options.explanation: In an isotonic solution, water moves equally in both directions, resulting in no net movement.

toLevel2.stem: A {{blank:1}} solution has a lower solute concentration than the cell, while a {{blank:2}} solution has a higher solute concentration.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: Hypotonic means the external solution has fewer solutes than inside the cell.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: Hypertonic means more solutes outside, not fewer.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: Isotonic means equal solute concentration on both sides.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: Hypertonic means the external solution has more solutes than inside the cell.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: Hypotonic means fewer solutes outside, not more.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: Isotonic means equal solute concentration, not higher.

toLevel2.stem: Tonicity describes how the {{blank:1}} of a solution determines the direction of {{blank:2}} across a membrane.

options.text: solute concentration
options.explanation: Tonicity is defined by the relative solute concentration of the external solution.

options.text: water temperature
options.explanation: Temperature is not the factor that defines tonicity.

options.text: membrane thickness
options.explanation: Membrane thickness does not define tonicity.

options.text: osmosis
options.explanation: Tonicity determines the direction and extent of osmosis across the membrane.

options.text: diffusion of solutes
options.explanation: Tonicity specifically relates to the movement of water by osmosis, not solute diffusion.

options.text: active transport
options.explanation: Active transport uses energy to move substances; tonicity relates to passive water movement.

toLevel2.stem: In an {{blank:1}} solution, the solute concentration outside equals the concentration {{blank:2}} the cell.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: Isotonic means equal solute concentration on both sides of the membrane.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: Hypotonic means lower solute concentration outside the cell.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: Hypertonic means higher solute concentration outside the cell.

options.text: inside
options.explanation: Tonicity compares the external solution to the internal environment of the cell.

options.text: around
options.explanation: Tonicity compares external concentration to the cell's internal concentration, not its surroundings.

options.text: beneath
options.explanation: Beneath is not a relevant spatial term for describing tonicity.

toLevel3.stem: Why is distilled water described as hypotonic relative to a red blood cell?

options.text: It contains no solutes while the cell contains dissolved salts and proteins
options.explanation: Distilled water has zero solute concentration, which is lower than the cell's internal solute concentration.

options.text: It has a higher salt concentration than the cytoplasm of the red blood cell
options.explanation: Distilled water has no salts; it is hypotonic, not hypertonic.

options.text: It has the same concentration of solutes as the inside of the red blood cell
options.explanation: Equal concentration would make it isotonic, not hypotonic.

options.text: It contains more dissolved gases than the interior of the red blood cell does
options.explanation: Dissolved gases are not the solutes that determine tonicity in this context.

toLevel3.stem: A student states that a 0.9% saline solution is isotonic to human red blood cells. What does this mean for water movement?

options.text: There is no net movement of water because concentrations are equal
options.explanation: An isotonic solution has the same solute concentration as the cell, so water moves equally in both directions with no net change.

options.text: Water rushes into the cells rapidly because saline is always hypotonic
options.explanation: 0.9% saline is isotonic to red blood cells, not hypotonic.

options.text: Water leaves the cells quickly because saline has more solute than cells
options.explanation: At 0.9%, the saline is isotonic and does not cause net water loss.

options.text: All water movement stops completely because the membrane seals itself shut
options.explanation: Water molecules still cross the membrane; there is simply no net movement.

toLevel3.stem: Why is it important to define tonicity relative to the cell rather than to pure water?

options.text: Because the direction of osmosis depends on the solute difference between the solution and cell
options.explanation: Osmosis depends on the relative concentration difference, so tonicity must be defined relative to the cell's internal environment.

options.text: Because pure water is always hypertonic to every type of cell without exception
options.explanation: Pure water is always hypotonic to cells because it has no solutes.

options.text: Because the cell membrane changes its structure depending on what is dissolved in water
options.explanation: Membrane structure does not change with external solutes; tonicity is about concentration gradients.

options.text: Because all cells have identical internal solute concentrations regardless of type
options.explanation: Different cell types have different internal concentrations, which is why tonicity must be defined relative to each cell.

toLevel3.stem: How does the concept of free water concentration relate to tonicity?

options.text: A hypotonic solution has more free water than the cell, driving water inward
options.explanation: Lower solute concentration means more free water molecules, which move down their gradient into the cell.

options.text: Free water concentration is identical in all solutions regardless of solute levels
options.explanation: Increasing solute concentration decreases the proportion of free water molecules.

options.text: A hypertonic solution has more free water because solutes attract extra water from air
options.explanation: More solutes mean less free water, not more; solutes bind some water molecules.

options.text: Free water only exists in isotonic solutions because other solutions lack available water
options.explanation: Free water exists in all solutions; its relative concentration differs with solute levels.

toLevel3.stem: A cell is placed in a solution where it neither swells nor shrinks. What can be concluded about the solution?

options.text: The solution is isotonic to the cell
options.explanation: No change in cell volume indicates equal solute concentration inside and outside, which defines an isotonic solution.

options.text: The solution is hypotonic to the cell
options.explanation: A hypotonic solution would cause the cell to swell as water enters.

options.text: The solution is hypertonic to cell
options.explanation: A hypertonic solution would cause the cell to shrink as water leaves.

options.text: The cell membrane has stopped working
options.explanation: The membrane is still functioning; water moves equally in both directions in an isotonic solution.

toLevel3.stem: Why does a cell swell when placed in a hypotonic solution?

options.text: Water moves into the cell because there is more free water outside than inside
options.explanation: The lower solute concentration outside means more free water molecules, which diffuse into the cell by osmosis.

options.text: Solutes rush out of the cell leaving space for the membrane to expand outward
options.explanation: Swelling is caused by water entering the cell, not by solutes leaving it.

options.text: The membrane actively pumps water in using ATP energy from the mitochondria nearby
options.explanation: Osmosis is a passive process; the cell does not actively pump water in.

options.text: The solution pushes physically against the cell surface and forces it to inflate
options.explanation: Swelling results from osmotic water entry, not from physical pressure pushing on the cell.

toLevel3.stem: In a hypotonic solution, the free water concentration is higher outside the cell than inside.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Lower solute concentration outside means more free water molecules, which drives water into the cell.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This is correct; a hypotonic solution has more free water outside, causing net water movement into the cell.

toLevel3.stem: When a cell is placed in a hypertonic solution, water moves {{blank:1}} of the cell because the external solution has a {{blank:2}} solute concentration.

options.text: out
options.explanation: Water moves from the area of higher free water concentration (inside the cell) to lower (outside).

options.text: into
options.explanation: Water moves into the cell in a hypotonic solution, not a hypertonic one.

options.text: around
options.explanation: Water moves across the membrane, not around it, during osmosis.

options.text: higher
options.explanation: Hypertonic means the external solution has a higher solute concentration than the cell interior.

options.text: lower
options.explanation: Lower solute concentration outside would make the solution hypotonic.

options.text: equal
options.explanation: Equal concentration would make the solution isotonic.

toLevel3.stem: Distilled water is {{blank:1}} to most cells because it contains {{blank:2}} dissolved solutes.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: Distilled water has no solutes, making it hypotonic relative to cells that contain dissolved substances.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: Distilled water has zero solutes, so it cannot be hypertonic to any cell.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: Distilled water would only be isotonic to a cell with no internal solutes, which is unrealistic.

options.text: no
options.explanation: Distilled water has been purified to remove all solutes.

options.text: many
options.explanation: Distilled water is characterised by having no dissolved solutes.

options.text: excess
options.explanation: Distilled water contains no solutes, not an excess.

toLevel3.stem: Tonicity is defined relative to the {{blank:1}} of the cell, not relative to {{blank:2}}.

options.text: internal environment
options.explanation: Tonicity compares the external solution's solute concentration to the cell's own internal concentration.

options.text: external temperature
options.explanation: Temperature is not the reference for defining tonicity.

options.text: membrane structure
options.explanation: Membrane structure does not define tonicity; solute concentration does.

options.text: pure water
options.explanation: Tonicity is defined relative to the cell, not to a fixed reference like pure water.

options.text: other cells
options.explanation: While tonicity is not defined relative to other cells, the key contrast is that it is defined relative to the cell itself, not pure water.

options.text: the nucleus
options.explanation: The nucleus is an organelle; tonicity is compared to the cell's overall internal solute concentration.

toLevel4.stem: A patient receives an IV drip of 0.9% saline during surgery. Why is this concentration chosen rather than pure water?

options.text: 0.9% saline is isotonic to blood cells, preventing cell damage from osmosis
options.explanation: Isotonic saline matches the solute concentration of blood, so red blood cells neither swell nor shrink.

options.text: Pure water is hypertonic and would cause red blood cells to shrink on contact
options.explanation: Pure water is hypotonic, not hypertonic; it would cause cells to swell and potentially lyse.

options.text: Saline provides essential nutrients that pure water cannot supply to the cells
options.explanation: The primary reason is osmotic balance, not nutrition; saline prevents cell damage.

options.text: Pure water cannot dissolve in blood so it would form dangerous bubbles in vessels
options.explanation: Water is miscible with blood; the concern is osmotic damage to cells, not bubble formation.

toLevel4.stem: A student places red blood cells in three solutions: 0.2%, 0.9%, and 5% NaCl. In which solution would the cells lyse?

options.text: 0.2% NaCl because it is hypotonic to the cells
options.explanation: 0.2% NaCl has a lower solute concentration than the cells, causing water to enter by osmosis until the cells burst.

options.text: 5% NaCl because it is hypotonic to cells
options.explanation: 5% NaCl is hypertonic, not hypotonic; cells would crenate, not lyse.

options.text: 0.9% NaCl because it matches the cell concentration exactly
options.explanation: 0.9% NaCl is isotonic; cells remain unchanged.

options.text: All three solutions cause lysis equally
options.explanation: Only the hypotonic solution (0.2%) causes lysis; the others cause crenation or no change.

toLevel4.stem: A kidney dialysis machine uses a solution isotonic to blood plasma. What would happen if the solution were accidentally made hypertonic?

options.text: Water would leave the blood cells, causing them to shrink and crenate
options.explanation: A hypertonic dialysis solution would draw water out of blood cells by osmosis, causing crenation.

options.text: Blood cells would swell and burst because water would rush in from the solution
options.explanation: Swelling and bursting would occur with a hypotonic solution, not a hypertonic one.

options.text: Nothing would change because dialysis machines automatically correct concentration errors
options.explanation: The machine does not self-correct; incorrect tonicity would directly affect blood cells.

options.text: The blood cells would divide more rapidly due to the extra solutes in the solution
options.explanation: Red blood cells do not divide; hypertonic conditions cause crenation, not cell division.

toLevel4.stem: Fresh strawberries sprinkled with sugar begin to release juice. Which tonicity concept explains this?

options.text: Sugar creates a hypertonic environment drawing water out of the fruit cells
options.explanation: The high sugar concentration outside the cells is hypertonic, causing water to leave the cells by osmosis.

options.text: Sugar dissolves the cell membranes allowing cytoplasm to leak out of the cells
options.explanation: Sugar does not dissolve membranes; the juice is released due to osmotic water loss.

options.text: Sugar adds water to the strawberries because it contains hidden moisture within it
options.explanation: Granulated sugar is dry; the juice comes from water leaving the fruit cells by osmosis.

options.text: Sugar is hypotonic to the fruit cells and forces water into the surrounding tissue
options.explanation: Sugar creates a hypertonic environment; hypotonic would cause water to enter, not leave, the cells.

toLevel4.stem: Slugs shrivel when salt is sprinkled on them. Apply tonicity concepts to explain this observation.

options.text: Salt creates a hypertonic environment on the slug's surface, drawing water out
options.explanation: The high salt concentration is hypertonic relative to the slug's cells, causing water to leave by osmosis.

options.text: Salt chemically reacts with the slug's skin to dissolve its protective outer layer
options.explanation: The shrivelling is due to osmotic water loss, not a chemical reaction with the skin.

options.text: Salt is hypotonic to the slug's body fluids, causing water to flood into the cells
options.explanation: Salt creates a hypertonic environment; a hypotonic environment would cause swelling, not shrivelling.

options.text: Salt physically compresses the slug's body through its heavy weight and pressure
options.explanation: The small amount of salt does not exert significant pressure; the effect is osmotic.

toLevel4.stem: A biologist needs to observe cells under a microscope without altering their shape. Which solution should be used to mount the cells?

options.text: An isotonic solution matching the cells' internal concentration
options.explanation: An isotonic solution ensures no net water movement, preserving the natural shape of the cells.

options.text: Distilled water because it is the purest mounting medium available
options.explanation: Distilled water is hypotonic and would cause cells to swell, distorting their shape.

options.text: A concentrated salt solution to keep the cells firmly in place on the slide
options.explanation: A concentrated salt solution is hypertonic and would cause cells to shrink.

options.text: Any solution will work because cell shape is determined only by the cytoskeleton
options.explanation: Tonicity affects cell volume; a non-isotonic solution would change cell shape regardless of the cytoskeleton.

toLevel4.stem: A student places cells in a 2% sucrose solution. The cells shrink. The student then adds water until the solution is 0.5% sucrose. What happens next?

options.text: The cells swell as the diluted solution becomes hypotonic to the shrunken cells
options.explanation: Diluting the solution lowers the external solute concentration below the cell's internal level, so water re-enters.

options.text: The cells continue shrinking because once water is lost it cannot re-enter the cell
options.explanation: Osmosis is reversible; water will re-enter the cells when the external solution becomes hypotonic.

options.text: The cells remain the same size because sucrose is still present in the solution used
options.explanation: The concentration has changed; the cells respond to the new tonicity of the diluted solution.

options.text: The cells dissolve completely because diluting the solution destroys the cell membranes
options.explanation: Diluting the solution does not destroy membranes; cells recover by taking in water.

toLevel4.stem: IV fluids for patients use {{blank:1}} saline because it is {{blank:2}} to blood cells, preventing osmotic damage.

options.explanation: 0.9% NaCl matches the solute concentration of blood plasma.
10% saline is hypertonic and would cause red blood cells to crenate.
0.01% saline is far too dilute and would be hypotonic, causing cells to swell.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: An isotonic solution has the same solute concentration as the cells, preventing net water movement.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: A hypertonic solution would draw water out of blood cells.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: A hypotonic solution would cause water to enter blood cells, potentially causing lysis.

toLevel4.stem: Sprinkling salt on a slug creates a {{blank:1}} environment on its surface, causing {{blank:2}} to leave the slug's cells by osmosis.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: The high salt concentration is hypertonic relative to the slug's body fluids.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: A hypotonic environment would cause water to enter cells, not leave them.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: An isotonic environment would cause no net water movement.

options.text: water
options.explanation: Water moves out of cells by osmosis when the external concentration is higher.

options.text: salt
options.explanation: Salt is outside the slug; it is water that leaves the cells by osmosis.

options.text: proteins
options.explanation: Proteins do not leave cells by osmosis; it is water that moves across the membrane.

toLevel4.stem: Red blood cells placed in {{blank:1}} water would swell and burst because the water is {{blank:2}} to the cells.

options.text: distilled
options.explanation: Distilled water contains no solutes and is hypotonic to red blood cells.

options.text: salty
options.explanation: Salty water would be hypertonic, causing cells to shrink, not burst.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: Isotonic water would not cause any change in cell volume.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: Distilled water has no solutes, making it hypotonic relative to the cells.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: Hypertonic solutions cause cells to shrink, not swell.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: Isotonic solutions cause no net water movement.

toLevel5.stem: A cell biologist discovers a single-celled organism that survives in both freshwater (hypotonic) and saltwater (hypertonic) environments. What adaptation is most likely responsible?

options.text: The organism has mechanisms to actively regulate its internal solute concentration
options.explanation: Osmoregulation allows the organism to adjust internal solute levels to manage osmotic stress in varying environments.

options.text: The organism lacks a plasma membrane so osmosis cannot affect it at all
options.explanation: All living cells have a plasma membrane; without one, the cell could not survive.

options.text: The organism converts all its internal water to ice to prevent osmotic movement
options.explanation: Freezing internal water would kill the cell; osmoregulation is the actual mechanism.

options.text: The organism is not affected by osmosis because it is too small for water to enter
options.explanation: Cell size does not prevent osmosis; even very small cells experience osmotic effects.

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that tonicity and osmolarity are the same concept. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: Incorrect; tonicity considers only non-penetrating solutes while osmolarity includes all solutes
options.explanation: Tonicity describes the effect on cell volume and only accounts for solutes that cannot cross the membrane, whereas osmolarity measures total solute concentration.

options.text: Correct; both terms describe total solute concentration and are completely interchangeable
options.explanation: They differ because tonicity considers only non-penetrating solutes that affect cell volume.

options.text: Incorrect; osmolarity relates to water purity while tonicity relates to membrane thickness
options.explanation: Osmolarity measures total solute concentration; tonicity relates to non-penetrating solutes and cell volume.

options.text: Correct; the terms differ only in spelling but refer to exactly the same measurement
options.explanation: They are distinct concepts; tonicity specifically considers which solutes affect cell volume.

toLevel5.stem: A solution containing 0.3 M urea and 0.3 M NaCl surrounds a cell. Urea freely crosses the membrane but NaCl does not. What is the effective tonicity of this solution?

options.text: The tonicity depends only on NaCl since urea freely crosses the membrane
options.explanation: Tonicity considers only non-penetrating solutes; since urea crosses freely, only the NaCl concentration determines the osmotic effect on cell volume.

options.text: The solution is hypotonic because urea dilutes the overall solute concentration
options.explanation: Urea does not dilute the solution; it freely crosses the membrane and does not contribute to tonicity.

options.text: Both urea and NaCl contribute equally to the tonicity of this particular solution
options.explanation: Only non-penetrating solutes like NaCl contribute to tonicity; urea equilibrates across the membrane.

options.text: The tonicity cannot be determined because two different solutes are present together
options.explanation: Tonicity can be determined by considering only the non-penetrating solute (NaCl).

toLevel5.stem: A researcher claims that placing cells in an isotonic solution guarantees they will be healthy. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: Partially correct; isotonic conditions maintain volume but cells need nutrients and proper pH too
options.explanation: While isotonic conditions prevent osmotic damage, cell health also depends on nutrient supply, pH, temperature, and waste removal.

options.text: Completely correct; isotonic conditions are the only requirement for cell survival in any context
options.explanation: Cells require many conditions beyond isotonicity, including nutrients, oxygen, and appropriate temperature.

options.text: Completely incorrect; isotonic solutions are actually toxic to cells in all situations tested
options.explanation: Isotonic solutions maintain cell volume and are not toxic; the claim is only partially correct.

options.text: Partially correct; but only because isotonic solutions also provide all essential nutrients cells need
options.explanation: An isotonic solution does not necessarily contain nutrients; it only matches solute concentration.

toLevel5.stem: Marine fish constantly drink seawater and excrete excess salt. How does tonicity explain this behaviour?

options.text: Seawater is hypertonic to their body fluids, so they lose water by osmosis and must replace it
options.explanation: The high salt concentration of seawater draws water out of the fish's cells, requiring constant water intake.

options.text: Seawater is hypotonic to their body fluids, so they must drink to dilute internal salt levels
options.explanation: Seawater is hypertonic, not hypotonic, to marine fish body fluids.

options.text: Seawater is isotonic to their body fluids but they drink it for nutritional minerals only
options.explanation: If seawater were isotonic, there would be no osmotic need to drink constantly.

options.text: Marine fish drink seawater as a behavioural habit unrelated to osmosis or tonicity
options.explanation: The drinking behaviour is directly linked to osmotic water loss in a hypertonic environment.

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that freshwater fish face the opposite osmotic challenge to marine fish. Evaluate this claim and predict the consequence.

options.text: Correct; freshwater is hypotonic so water constantly enters, and fish must excrete dilute urine
options.explanation: Freshwater has fewer solutes than fish body fluids, so water enters by osmosis and the fish must excrete excess water.

options.text: Incorrect; freshwater fish face the same challenge as marine fish because water is always the same
options.explanation: Freshwater and seawater have very different solute concentrations, creating opposite osmotic challenges.

options.text: Correct; but freshwater fish solve this by drinking large volumes of water constantly
options.explanation: Freshwater fish actually avoid drinking water; they excrete excess water that enters by osmosis.

options.text: Incorrect; freshwater has no effect on fish cells because fish are immune to osmotic change
options.explanation: Fish are not immune to osmosis; freshwater fish must actively regulate their water balance.

toLevel5.stem: A cell is placed in a solution that is initially isotonic. Over time, the cell actively pumps solutes inward. How would the tonicity of the surrounding solution change relative to the cell?

options.text: The solution becomes hypotonic relative to the cell as internal solute concentration rises
options.explanation: As the cell increases its internal solute concentration, the external solution has relatively fewer solutes, making it hypotonic.

options.text: The solution remains isotonic because the cell cannot change external concentrations at all
options.explanation: While the external concentration may not change much, the cell's internal concentration rises, changing the relative tonicity.

options.text: The solution becomes hypertonic because the cell's active transport pushes solutes outward
options.explanation: The cell is pumping solutes inward, increasing internal concentration and making the external solution relatively hypotonic.

options.text: The tonicity does not change because active transport has no connection to osmotic pressure
options.explanation: Active transport changes internal solute concentration, which directly affects the relative tonicity.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that a 1 M glucose solution and a 1 M NaCl solution have the same tonicity. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: Incorrect; NaCl dissociates into two ions, effectively doubling the solute particle concentration
options.explanation: NaCl splits into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, producing roughly twice the number of solute particles as the same molarity of glucose.

options.text: Correct; both solutions have the same molarity so their tonicity must be identical
options.explanation: Tonicity depends on the number of solute particles, and NaCl produces more particles per mole than glucose.

options.text: Incorrect; glucose is always hypertonic regardless of concentration because it is a larger molecule
options.explanation: Molecular size does not determine tonicity; the number of dissolved particles does.

options.text: Correct; tonicity depends on the mass of solute, and both solutions contain the same mass
options.explanation: Tonicity depends on the number of solute particles, not the mass; NaCl dissociates into more particles.

toLevel5.stem: Marine fish lose water by osmosis because seawater is {{blank:1}} to their body fluids, so they must constantly {{blank:2}} to compensate.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: Seawater has a higher solute concentration than marine fish body fluids.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: Seawater is not hypotonic; it has more dissolved salts than fish body fluids.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: Seawater is not isotonic to most marine fish; it is hypertonic.

options.text: drink seawater
options.explanation: Marine fish drink seawater to replace water lost by osmosis and then excrete the excess salt.

options.text: excrete water
options.explanation: Marine fish are losing water, not gaining it; they need to drink, not excrete.

options.text: absorb salt
options.explanation: Marine fish already gain excess salt; they need to replace lost water by drinking.

toLevel5.stem: NaCl dissociates into {{blank:1}} ions in solution, so a 1 M NaCl solution has a greater effective tonicity than a 1 M {{blank:2}} solution.

options.text: two
options.explanation: NaCl dissociates into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, producing two particles per formula unit.

options.text: one
options.explanation: NaCl dissociates into two ions, not one.

options.text: three
options.explanation: NaCl produces two ions per formula unit, not three.

options.text: glucose
options.explanation: Glucose does not dissociate, so 1 M glucose produces fewer solute particles than 1 M NaCl.

options.text: sodium chloride
options.explanation: Comparing NaCl to itself would show equal tonicity; the comparison is with a non-dissociating solute.

options.text: calcium chloride
options.explanation: CaCl₂ dissociates into three ions, which would have even greater tonicity than NaCl.
